title: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis, usually called PrEP, is medicine taken by a person who does not have HIV to lower the chance of getting HIV. It is for people who may be exposed to HIV, for example through sex without a condom or through shared injection equipment. PrEP is not a vaccine and it is not treatment for HIV. It is a prevention tool that only works while it is being taken as directed.

PrEP works by keeping enough medicine in the body to stop HIV from establishing an infection after an exposure. The most common form is a daily pill containing two antiretroviral medicines. A long-acting injection given every two months is another option in places where it is available. A clinician checks that the person does not already have HIV before PrEP starts, and repeats HIV testing during follow-up, because starting PrEP while HIV-positive without full treatment can lead to drug resistance.

When taken as prescribed, daily oral PrEP lowers the risk of sexually acquired HIV by about 99 percent, according to CDC estimates from clinical studies. It is much less protective when doses are missed, which is why adherence matters so much. The injection form showed very high protection in trials when injections were kept on schedule. PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections or against pregnancy, so condoms and other protection are still discussed at follow-up visits.

PrEP is available through clinics, sexual-health services, and in some places through pharmacies or telehealth. Cost and coverage vary, and assistance programs exist in many countries, so a clinic can explain local options. PrEP is not suitable for everyone: kidney health, hepatitis B status, and other medicines are checked first. Anyone considering PrEP should see a clinician or an HIV testing service to discuss whether it fits, how to take it, and when to test.

print('4. Book follow-up: HIV test, kidney check, and STI screen on schedule.')

print('PrEP lowers risk greatly when taken as prescribed; it is not fully effective and does not protect against other STIs.')
print('See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.')

title: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Post-exposure prophylaxis, called PEP, is emergency medicine taken after a possible exposure to HIV. It is for situations such as sex without a condom with a partner who may have HIV, a condom breaking, a sexual assault, or a needle-stick injury. PEP is not a single morning-after pill. It is a full course of medicine taken for 28 days.

PEP works by attacking HIV before it can establish a lasting infection, which is why speed matters so much. It must be started within 72 hours of the exposure, and it works best when started as soon as possible, ideally within hours. A clinician or emergency service assesses the risk, tests for HIV and other infections, and prescribes a combination of antiretroviral medicines if PEP is appropriate.

PEP lowers the risk of HIV after an exposure, but it cannot be relied on to work every time. Starting late, missing doses, or stopping early all reduce its value. Side effects such as nausea and tiredness are common and are one reason people stop early, so follow-up support matters. After the course, follow-up HIV testing is arranged to check the result, because only testing can show whether infection occurred.

PEP is available through emergency departments, urgent-care clinics, and sexual-health services, and in many places it is available day and night. Because the 72-hour window closes quickly, anyone who thinks they may have been exposed should seek care immediately rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Cost should never be a reason to delay: emergency services can explain coverage and assistance options. See a clinician or an emergency service right away after a possible exposure.

title: Condoms
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Condoms are thin sheaths worn during sex that block HIV and other germs from passing between partners. External condoms fit over the penis, and internal condoms fit inside the vagina or anus. When used correctly every time, condoms are one of the most reliable and widely available ways to prevent HIV transmission during sex.

A condom works as a physical barrier: it keeps semen, vaginal fluid, and other body fluids from contacting a partner's mucous membranes, where HIV can enter the body. For this barrier to work, the condom must be the right size, undamaged, and within its expiry date. It must be put on before any genital contact, used with a suitable lubricant if needed, and held at the base when withdrawing so nothing leaks.

Condoms are highly effective when used correctly and consistently, but they are not fully effective in real life because they can break, slip, or be used incorrectly. Studies of consistent and correct use show very high protection against HIV, while typical use, which includes mistakes and skipped use, protects less well. Condoms also lower the risk of many other sexually transmitted infections and, for vaginal sex, of pregnancy, which is an extra benefit no medicine-based method offers on its own.

Condoms are available cheaply or free from clinics, pharmacies, community organizations, and vending machines in many places, without a prescription. They should be stored away from heat and sharp objects and checked for damage before use. Anyone unsure about correct use can ask a clinician or a sexual-health service for a demonstration. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about combining condoms with other prevention methods.

title: Regular HIV Testing
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Regular HIV testing means getting tested for HIV on a routine basis, not only when symptoms appear. Many people with HIV feel well for years, so testing is the only way to know one's status. Knowing one's status early means treatment can start sooner, which protects health and, once treatment suppresses the virus, prevents onward transmission.

Testing is usually a blood test or a mouth swab, done at a clinic, a testing service, or with a home test kit where available. Laboratory tests look for antibodies the body makes against HIV, for parts of the virus itself, or for both. Rapid tests give results in under an hour, while laboratory tests take longer but are very accurate. A positive screening result is always confirmed with further testing before anyone is told they have HIV.

No test can detect HIV immediately after infection. This gap is called the window period: it takes time for the virus or antibodies to reach detectable levels. Modern laboratory tests usually detect HIV within a few weeks of infection, but a clinician may advise a repeat test after the window period to be sure. Testing regularly, rather than once, is therefore important for people with ongoing risk.

Testing is available at clinics, sexual-health services, community testing events, and by mail or home kit in many places, often free and confidential. Some services offer anonymous testing. Anyone who is unsure when to test, or who has had a recent possible exposure, should see a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on which test and when to repeat it.

title: Treatment as Prevention and U=U
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Treatment as prevention means that a person with HIV who takes antiretroviral treatment and reaches an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV to sexual partners. This is summed up as U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable. It is one of the most important facts in modern HIV prevention, and it is also a strong reason to test early and start treatment.

HIV treatment works by stopping the virus from copying itself in the body. When treatment is taken every day, the amount of virus in the blood, called the viral load, falls until standard tests cannot detect it. At that point the person still has HIV and must keep taking treatment, but the virus is too suppressed to be passed on during sex. This only holds while the viral load stays undetectable, which is checked with regular blood tests.

Large studies of couples where one partner had HIV and the other did not found no linked sexual transmissions once the partner with HIV was durably undetectable. That is strong evidence, but it comes with conditions: treatment must be taken consistently, viral load must be monitored, and any treatment interruption can let the virus return. U=U applies to sexual transmission; it does not cover transmission through shared injection equipment or from parent to child, which have their own prevention steps.

Treatment is available through HIV clinics and, in many places, through primary care, with costs covered by public programs or insurance in many countries. Starting treatment soon after diagnosis is now standard advice. Anyone who has HIV, or who thinks they may, should see a clinician or an HIV testing service promptly to discuss testing and treatment, and partners can ask about prevention options at the same visit.

title: Needle and Syringe Safety and Harm-Reduction Services
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

HIV can pass when injection equipment is shared, because blood left in a needle or syringe can carry the virus to the next person. Needle and syringe safety means using a new, sterile needle and syringe for every injection, never sharing any injection equipment, and disposing of used equipment safely. This applies to any injection, including drug injection and any other injection outside a medical setting.

Harm-reduction services, often called syringe services programs, provide sterile equipment, safe disposal containers, HIV and hepatitis testing, and links to health care and drug treatment. They do not require a person to stop using drugs before receiving help. Many also offer wound care, vaccinations, and overdose-prevention supplies. The approach is practical: reduce the harm of injection while keeping the door open to treatment whenever the person is ready.

Syringe services programs are supported by strong public-health evidence: communities with these programs see fewer new HIV and hepatitis infections among people who inject drugs, and more people linked to testing and treatment. No single service removes all risk, and sharing any part of the equipment, including cookers, filters, or water, can still pass infection, so sterile equipment for every item matters. Combining syringe services with HIV testing, PrEP where appropriate, and treatment for those with HIV gives the strongest protection.

These services are available in many cities through public-health departments and community organizations, though laws and availability vary by place. Services are usually confidential and low-threshold, meaning little paperwork and no requirement to be abstinent. Anyone who injects drugs, or who knows someone who does, can contact a local syringe service or a clinician for sterile supplies, testing, and advice. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for testing and for links to local harm-reduction services.

title: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

A parent with HIV can pass the virus to a baby during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission is the set of steps that makes this very unlikely: testing during pregnancy, HIV treatment for the pregnant person, careful planning of the birth, medicine for the baby after birth, and guidance about infant feeding.

The steps work together. Testing early in pregnancy finds HIV in time for treatment to suppress the virus before birth. Antiretroviral treatment lowers the amount of virus in the blood, which lowers the chance of passing it to the baby. During birth, the care team takes extra steps to reduce exposure, and after birth the baby receives preventive medicine for a period set by the clinician. Feeding advice depends on the setting: where safe alternatives are available, avoiding breastfeeding may be advised, while in other settings continued breastfeeding with treatment is advised, because the risks differ.

Without any prevention steps, the chance of a baby acquiring HIV is roughly one in six to nearly one in two, depending on feeding. With testing, treatment, and infant medicine, the chance falls to a very small fraction, below 1 to 2 percent in settings with full access to care. The result depends on starting treatment early, taking it consistently, and keeping every follow-up appointment for parent and baby.

Care is available through antenatal clinics, which routinely offer HIV testing as part of pregnancy care, often with an opt-out approach. Testing and treatment are usually free or covered in many countries. Anyone who is pregnant, or planning a pregnancy, and who does not know their HIV status should see a clinician or an HIV testing service early in pregnancy to discuss testing and, if needed, treatment planning.

title: Partner Services and Notification
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Partner services are confidential health-department or clinic services that help a person with HIV, or another sexually transmitted infection, let their partners know they may have been exposed. The goal is simple: partners get tested, and if they need treatment or prevention, they get it quickly. This protects the partners' health and helps stop further transmission.

There are several ways to notify a partner. A person can tell partners themselves, with coaching and support from the service. Or the service can contact partners without revealing who named them, so the partner learns of a possible exposure but not the source. The service can also arrange testing and, where appropriate, prevention such as PrEP or emergency PEP for a partner with a recent exposure.

Partner services work best when they are confidential and voluntary, and when testing and care are offered at the same time as notification. Studies show that assisted notification finds more partners and more new diagnoses than leaving people entirely on their own. The limits are real: some partners cannot be reached, some decline testing, and notification can be sensitive or unsafe in relationships involving violence, so services plan for safety first and never force disclosure.

Partner services are available through health departments and sexual-health clinics, often free. Anyone newly diagnosed, or anyone who learns a partner may have HIV, can ask a clinic about partner services. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for confidential advice about notification, testing, and safety planning.

title: Education and Stigma Reduction
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Education and stigma reduction means giving people accurate information about HIV and challenging the shame and fear that surround it. Stigma keeps people from testing, from telling partners, and from taking treatment openly. When stigma falls, more people test, more people start treatment, and prevention works better.

Good education explains the basics in plain language: how HIV is and is not transmitted, that treatment lets people with HIV live long healthy lives, and that a person with an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV to sexual partners. It corrects common myths, such as the idea that HIV spreads through hugging, sharing food, or mosquito bites, which it does not. Education works best when it comes from trusted sources, including schools, clinics, community groups, and people living with HIV themselves.

Anti-stigma programs have been shown to improve attitudes and willingness to test, though changing deep attitudes takes time and repeated contact. Education alone does not prevent HIV: information must be paired with access to condoms, testing, treatment, and prevention medicines. Programs that only hand out facts without services, or that use fear and shame, tend to fail or backfire.

Education resources are available from health departments, schools, clinics, and community organizations, often free. Anyone who wants reliable information, or who faces stigma when seeking care, can ask a clinic or testing service for local programs and support groups. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for accurate information and for links to supportive services.

ED = 'elliptical'
QUESTIONS = [

    ('A person with an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV to sexual partners.', 'FACT'),

    ('Testing is the only way to know your HIV status.', 'FACT'),

title: Safer-Sex Communication
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Safer-sex communication means talking with a partner about HIV and sexual health before sex: recent testing, condom use, PrEP or treatment, and what each person is comfortable with. These conversations are a prevention tool in their own right, because protection only happens when both partners agree to it.

A good conversation is short, direct, and early, not in the heat of the moment. It can cover when each person last tested, whether condoms will be used, whether either person uses PrEP or HIV treatment, and what to do if a condom breaks. Agreeing a plan beforehand makes it much easier to follow through. If a partner refuses condoms or testing, that is important information, and the other person can decide not to proceed.

Communication supports every other method: condoms get used when both partners expect them, testing happens when partners encourage each other, and treatment adherence is easier with a supportive partner. Communication alone, however, does not block transmission, and it cannot verify what a partner says about their status or treatment. Trust helps, but testing and protection are still needed.

Communication skills can be learned from clinics, counseling services, and community programs, which often offer practice scripts and role-play. Anyone who finds these conversations difficult, or who faces pressure or coercion around sex, can ask a clinician or a counseling service for support. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice and for help with difficult conversations.

title: Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Voluntary medical male circumcision is the surgical removal of the foreskin of the penis, done in a clinic by trained staff, for men who choose it. It is offered in some countries with high HIV rates as one part of a package of HIV prevention, always with counseling, testing, and condoms. It is voluntary: no one should be pressured into it.

Circumcision lowers HIV risk because the inner foreskin contains many of the cells HIV targets, and it is prone to small tears during sex. Removing it reduces the surface through which HIV can enter. The procedure is done with pain relief, takes under an hour, and healing takes several weeks, during which sex must be avoided so the wound can close.

Three large trials in Africa found that circumcision reduced female-to-male HIV transmission by about 60 percent. That is a large reduction, but it is partial protection, not full protection: circumcised men can still acquire HIV, and condoms and other prevention are still needed. The evidence is for heterosexual transmission to men; it does not show the same benefit for other transmission routes, and it does not protect female partners directly except through lower prevalence in men over time.

The service is available in clinics in countries that run voluntary circumcision programs, usually free, with counseling and HIV testing offered at the same visit. Risks include bleeding, infection, and poor healing, which are uncommon with trained providers and proper follow-up. Anyone considering it should see a clinician or an HIV testing service to discuss benefits, risks, and the healing period.

title: Lubricant Safety with Condoms
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Lubricant, sometimes called lube, reduces friction during sex, which makes condoms less likely to break and sex more comfortable. But not every lubricant is safe with every condom. Using the wrong kind can weaken the condom and undo its protection, so choosing the right lubricant matters.

Water-based and silicone-based lubricants are safe with latex condoms. Oil-based products, including cooking oil, baby oil, petroleum jelly, and many body lotions, damage latex and can cause condoms to break. For non-latex condoms made of polyurethane, most lubricants are safe, but silicone-based lubricant should not be used with silicone toys, and the product label should always be checked.

Lubricant improves condom effectiveness in practice by reducing breakage, especially for anal sex, where natural lubrication is lower. It does not itself block HIV, and a lubricant with a numbing agent should be used cautiously, since reduced feeling can hide pain that signals a condom problem or injury. Lubricants do not replace condoms, testing, or other prevention.

Lubricants are available at pharmacies, clinics, and community organizations, often free alongside condoms. Clinics that distribute condoms usually stock compatible lubricants as well, and community organizations often give both away together, so asking for the matching product is easy. Anyone unsure which product suits their condoms can check the label or ask a clinician or sexual-health service. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on condoms and lubricants.

title: Testing Frequency Guidance
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Testing frequency guidance answers a practical question: how often should a person test for HIV? The answer depends on risk. People with ongoing risk test more often, while people with little risk test less often, but everyone is advised to test at least once.

Public-health guidance in many countries advises that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested at least once as part of routine health care. People who are sexually active, especially men who have sex with men, people with partners who have HIV, people who inject drugs, and people with other sexually transmitted infections, are advised to test at least once a year. People at higher ongoing risk, such as those with multiple partners or partners of unknown status, are advised to test every three to six months.

Frequent testing works because it shortens the time between acquiring HIV and starting treatment, which protects health and prevents onward transmission. Testing more often than needed is not harmful, but it can create anxiety, and a test taken too soon after an exposure may need repeating after the window period. Frequency guidance is therefore paired with advice on which test to take and when to repeat it.

Testing is available at clinics, sexual-health services, community events, and by home kit in many places. Anyone unsure how often to test can ask a clinician or testing service to set a personal schedule. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on a testing schedule for your situation.

title: Linkage to Care After a Positive Result
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Linkage to care means connecting a person who tests positive for HIV to medical care quickly, ideally within days. A positive screening result is first confirmed with further laboratory testing. Then the person meets an HIV care team, starts treatment, and gets support for partners, prevention, and everyday life with HIV.

The first visit covers a lot: confirming the result, checking overall health and other infections, discussing treatment options, and planning follow-up. Treatment usually starts soon after diagnosis, often the same day or within days, because early treatment protects health and, once the virus is suppressed, prevents sexual transmission. Counseling covers telling partners, coping with the news, and practical matters such as work and privacy.

Rapid linkage works: people linked quickly start treatment sooner, reach undetectable viral loads sooner, and stay in care longer. The main failures are delays: people who are not contacted after a positive result, who face transport or cost barriers, or who fear stigma may never reach care. Services that book the first appointment at the testing visit, offer peer support, and follow up on missed appointments do much better.

Care is available through HIV clinics and, in many places, primary care, with costs covered by public programs or insurance in many countries. Anyone who receives a positive result, or who has not been contacted after one, should contact a clinic promptly. See a clinician or an HIV testing service immediately after a positive result to arrange confirmatory testing and care.

title: PrEP Adherence Support
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

PrEP adherence support means the help that keeps a person taking PrEP as prescribed: daily pills on schedule, or injections on time. PrEP only protects while drug levels in the body are high enough, so missed doses are the main reason PrEP fails. Support turns a prescription into real protection.

Support starts with a routine: taking the pill at the same time each day, linked to an existing habit such as brushing teeth or a morning meal. Reminders help, whether a phone alarm, a pill box, or a message from the clinic. Regular follow-up visits check HIV status, kidney health, and side effects, and give a chance to talk about problems such as nausea, stigma, or difficulty getting refills. For injections, the clinic books the next appointment before the person leaves.

Adherence support is highly effective at its job: studies show that people with good support take more doses, and people who take PrEP as prescribed are far better protected than people who take it irregularly. Support cannot make PrEP fully effective, and it cannot fix supply interruptions or cost barriers on its own, which is why clinics also work on access. Side effects usually settle within weeks, and a clinician can help if they do not.

Support is available through PrEP clinics, pharmacies, and community programs, often including text reminders and peer support. Anyone on PrEP who is missing doses, or who is thinking of stopping, should talk to their clinician rather than stopping quietly, because stopping changes protection and, for injections, needs a plan for the tail period. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for adherence help and follow-up.

title: Community Outreach Programs
body:
Language used in this record. HIV is the virus. AIDS is the syndrome that can develop when HIV is not treated, so prevention here means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV: the rare stem-cell transplant cases reported in research are exceptions studied in hospitals, not treatments available to the public. No prevention method in this database is fully effective on its own; each one lowers risk, and how well it works depends on using it correctly and consistently. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

Community outreach programs bring HIV prevention to people where they live, work, and gather, instead of waiting for people to come to a clinic. Outreach workers, often peers from the same community, offer information, condoms, HIV testing, and links to PrEP, treatment, and harm-reduction services at bars, clubs, shelters, workplaces, and mobile units.

Outreach works because it removes the barriers that keep people from clinics: distance, opening hours, cost, mistrust, and stigma. A familiar face offering a test in a comfortable place is easier to accept than a formal clinic visit. Outreach also reaches people who do not see themselves at risk and would never seek testing on their own. Peer workers are central: they speak the community's language, understand its concerns, and are trusted in ways outsiders are not.

Outreach programs have been shown to increase testing uptake and linkage to prevention and care, particularly among groups with the least clinic contact. Outreach alone does not prevent HIV: it works by connecting people to condoms, testing, PrEP, and treatment. Programs that only hand out leaflets without testing or referral links achieve much less, and programs must be sustained, since one-off events rarely change behavior for long.

Outreach is available through health departments, community organizations, and mobile testing units, often free. Anyone who wants prevention services but cannot easily reach a clinic, or who wants to help their community, can contact a local outreach program. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for links to outreach and community programs near you.
